5.6. Elliptic Regularity and Solution Operators🔗

A weak solution from the previous two sections is, so far, only an element of H^1_0(\Omega). It is more regular when coefficients, forcing, and boundary allow, and the improved solution map is a bounded linear operator. The engine is Nirenberg's difference-quotient method: testing the weak equation with a second difference quotient of the solution, ellipticity bounds the difference quotients of the gradient in L^2, and the difference-quotient criterion of the Sobolev chapter turns those bounds into a second weak derivative. Cutoffs localize the argument to the interior, the flattening charts of an operational C^2 boundary atlas carry it to the boundary, and a finite partition of unity assembles the global H^2 estimate for the homogeneous Dirichlet problem.

Linearity of the equation and uniqueness of the weak solution make the regular solution map linear; the closed graph theorem makes it continuous. The resulting H^2 and higher-order solution operators have trajectory and Bochner lifts for applying the spatial estimates to time-dependent data.

5.6.1. Interior and Boundary Regularity🔗

Elliptic regularity reconnects the variational and classical theories: a weak solution produced by Lax–Milgram gains as many Sobolev derivatives as the coefficients and data permit.

Difference quotients are defined on H^1 functions, even when pointwise derivatives are unavailable, and their product identities separate the solution, coefficients, and cutoffs. They regularize within the energy space, with no mollification. Cutoff functions introduce commutator terms, boundary charts introduce Jacobian factors, and lower-order coefficients introduce additional forcing.

Evans (2010, Sections 6.3.1–6.3.2, pp. 327–343) proves interior H^2 regularity for arbitrary H^1 weak solutions, global boundary regularity for homogeneous Dirichlet solutions, higher-order Sobolev regularity, and smoothness under smooth data. We prove Evans's compact-set interior theorem for arbitrary H^1 weak solutions, and also a zero-trace version localized by an atlas cutoff, which is the form the global Dirichlet assembly uses.

5.6.1.1. Operational Boundary Geometry🔗

Boundary regularity needs more than an abstract smooth-boundary label: the proof differentiates flattening maps, transfers weak derivatives, and sums localized estimates through a finite partition of unity. The operational atlases record exactly that data, with concrete instances for the interval and every positive-dimensional Euclidean unit ball.

This reuses the geometry of Sobolev extension, but asks it to do more. Extension continues a function whose first derivatives are already controlled. Boundary regularity must obtain an additional derivative from the equation. Flattening transforms the coefficients as well as the function, and differentiating that transformed equation requires extra chart derivatives. We use explicit atlases so that this extra cost is part of the hypotheses, even on the familiar interval and ball.

✓L∃∀N

A finite boundary cover consists of bounded open neighborhoods U_i whose union contains the frontier \partial\Omega of a bounded open domain. Adding \Omega as the interior member gives a finite open cover of \overline\Omega. Mathlib's smooth partition-of-unity theorem then canonically supplies compactly supported interior and boundary test functions subordinate to those sets and summing to one on \Omega.

A cover alone carries no analytic information about the boundary. The flattening charts add it: each boundary patch receives a map identifying the domain locally with the upper half-space, and the differentiability class of these maps is what distinguishes the C^1 extension atlas from the C^2 regularity atlas.

After the subordinate cutoffs are fixed, one attaches a flattening chart to each boundary neighborhood. Only the compact support of the corresponding cutoff must lie in the chart source. Globally represented C^1 charts produce an extension atlas, while C^2 charts produce the operational boundary atlas used by elliptic regularity.

For \Omega=(-1,1), the affine endpoint maps \Phi_-(x)=x+1 and \Phi_+(x)=1-x identify neighborhoods of the two boundary points with neighborhoods in the upper half-line (0,\infty). Both maps are affine with affine inverses, hence smooth to every finite order. Together with an interior patch and a finite subordinate partition of unity, they furnish the operational C^2 boundary atlas used by the global elliptic and parabolic regularity theorems.

In higher dimensions the unit ball is the model domain, and its atlas is assembled in two stages. The first stage is the cover: finitely many signed coordinate caps containing the sphere, together with a subordinate partition of unity; each cap is later flattened by a graph chart.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

In every positive dimension, the Euclidean unit ball has a finite cover by 2n signed coordinate caps together with a smooth subordinate partition of unity. The interior and boundary cutoffs have compact support in their assigned sets and sum exactly to one on the ball. Its global defining function \rho(x)=1-\lVert x\rVert^2 is smooth, is positive exactly in the ball, and has nonzero radial differential on the unit sphere.

The caps cover the sphere: a point of the unit sphere is nonzero, so at least one coordinate is either positive or negative, and the identity \sum_j x_j^2=1 shows that the remaining tangential coordinates have squared norm strictly less than one, placing the point in the corresponding signed cap. Together with the open ball, these finitely many caps cover the closed ball. Mathlib's smooth partition-of-unity theorem supplies the cutoffs, and boundedness of the cover sets makes their supports compact.

    theorem SobolevSpace.Boundary.Atlas.UnitBall.radialCovector_ne_zero_of_mem_sphere
  (n : ℕ) {x : ℝ^n} (hx : x ∈ Metric.sphere 0 1) : (innerSL ℝ) x ≠ 0
    theorem SobolevSpace.Boundary.Atlas.UnitBall.radialCovector_ne_zero_of_mem_sphere
  (n : ℕ) {x : ℝ^n}
  (hx : x ∈ Metric.sphere 0 1) :
  (innerSL ℝ) x ≠ 0

    The radial covector is nonzero at every point of the unit sphere. In combination with hasStrictFDerivAt_norm_sq, this is the nondegeneracy input for applying the inverse-function theorem to the defining function.

On each cap the sphere is the graph of a height function over the tangential coordinates, and subtracting or adding that height in the normal coordinate flattens the cap. The constructor requires chart representatives differentiable on all of \mathbb R^n, so the local height \sqrt{1-\lVert x'\rVert^2} is replaced by a globally smooth function agreeing with it on a slightly smaller tangential cylinder.

Proof for Theorem 5.176
uses 0

The flattening maps preserve every tangential coordinate and replace the normal coordinate by g(x')-x_n or g(x')+x_n. Direct coordinate calculations give their inverses. The inequalities x_n<g(x') and x_n>-g(x'), respectively, are equivalent to positivity of the flattened normal coordinate. Componentwise calculus proves the required differentiability. Restricting each global homeomorphism to a bounded open source gives a bounded partial chart because the image of the compact source closure is bounded. For the sphere, the local height \sqrt{1-\lVert x'\rVert^2} is smooth on the region where its radicand is positive; Mathlib's relative smooth-extension theorem produces a globally smooth function agreeing with it on any strictly smaller closed tangential cylinder.

Feeding the cap cover and the graph charts into the constructor gives the concrete C^2 atlas on which the global regularity theorems can be instantiated for the unit ball in every positive dimension.

5.6.1.2. From Local H² Pieces to Global Regularity🔗

The H^2 proof has two analytic pieces. Interior cutoffs permit ordinary difference quotients, while boundary cutoffs are flattened to the half-space so tangential derivatives can be estimated and the normal derivative recovered from the equation. The finite atlas then reassembles those local representatives into one global Sobolev field.

The difference-quotient bootstrap works as follows. Given a weak solution u\in H^1_0(\Omega) of -\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f, choose a direction e_k and form the second-order difference quotient \Delta_h^{-k}\Delta_h^k u where \Delta_h^k u(x)=(u(x+he_k)-u(x))/h. Testing the weak equation against \varphi=-\Delta_h^{-k}(\eta^2\Delta_h^k u) (where \eta is a smooth interior cutoff) and using the discrete product rule gives

\alpha\int|\nabla(\eta\Delta_h^k u)|^2 \leq C\bigl(\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}^2+\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^2\bigr).

The constant hides the cost of localization. For concentric balls \overline{B_r}\subset B_R\subset\Omega, choose \eta=1 on B_r and supported in B_R, with |\nabla\eta|\le C_n/(R-r). The product rule introduces this factor into the estimate. Thus interior regularity controls derivatives on a smaller region from data on a larger one, and the bound deteriorates when the gap closes. It requires no boundary trace for an arbitrary local weak solution; extending the conclusion to the whole domain requires a separate boundary argument.

Choose sufficiently small nonzero steps h_m\to0. The product rule and this estimate bound the localized difference quotients of the first derivatives in L^2. Weak compactness supplies a weak limit along an ultrafilter containing every tail of the sequence. Discrete integration by parts identifies each limit as a second weak derivative where \eta=1. Repeating this in every coordinate gives an H^2 representative on that interior region. Near the boundary the argument is more delicate: one can only take tangential difference quotients directly, and the normal second derivative is then recovered algebraically from the equation using ellipticity of the leading coefficient (Evans, 2010, pp. 327–340; Gilbarg and Trudinger (2001), Section 8.3).

    This is the one-dimensional case of H² regularity for the Laplacian; unlike the multidimensional theorems, it needs no difference quotients or boundary charts.

Proof for Theorem 5.178
uses 0

The weak Poisson identity says directly that the first weak derivative of u has weak derivative -f. The second-derivative assembly theorem then combines the base value, first derivative, and second derivative into one W^{2,2} representative.

In one dimension the second derivative is read directly from the equation. For variable principal coefficients the difference-quotient argument is needed, and it gives regularity on compact subsets of the domain.

    Evans §6.3.1, interior H² regularity for general weak solutions.

    Let u ∈ H¹(Ω) solve a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation weakly, without any boundary condition. Every compact subset K ⊆ Ω has an open neighborhood V ⊆ Ω on which u has an H²(V) representative.

    The proof uses two nested cutoffs. The outer cutoff turns u into an H¹₀(Ω) solution with an L² commutator forcing. The inner cutoff lies where the outer cutoff equals one, so the zero-trace difference-quotient theorem produces an H² representative of the original field near K.

Proof for Theorem 5.179
uses 0

Choose an outer cutoff equal to one near K. Its product with u belongs to H^1_0(\Omega) and satisfies a divergence-form equation whose commutator forcing lies in L^2. Choose a second cutoff inside the region where the first equals one and apply the quantitative zero-trace difference-quotient theorem. On the second cutoff region the localized field and u agree almost everywhere, so the resulting H^2 field represents the original weak solution near K.

Passing to higher orders requires differentiating the equation, which is done on localized solutions with zero trace. The cutoff lemma provides those localized solutions at every Sobolev order in a single statement.

Let k>0 and let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open. Suppose a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega), f\in W^{k,2}(\Omega), and u\in W^{k+1,2}(\Omega) represents an H^1_0(\Omega) weak solution of

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f.

For every smooth compactly supported cutoff \rho on \mathbb R^n, the product w=\rho u has an H^1_0(\Omega) representative and there is a forcing G\in W^{k,2}(\Omega), supported where \rho is supported, such that

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j w)=G

weakly on \Omega.

    For positive k, cutoff localization sends coefficients and a zero-trace solution of order k + 1, together with forcing of order k, to a supported W^{k,2} commutator forcing satisfying the localized weak equation.

Proof for Theorem 5.180
uses 0

Apply first-order cutoff localization to obtain the weak equation for \rho u. Its forcing is the original forcing multiplied by \rho together with the two coefficient-cutoff commutators. Repeated weak Leibniz rules, finite derivative-word sums, and the general W^{k,\infty}\times W^{k,2}\to W^{k,2} multiplier theorem put every term in W^{k,2}. The cutoff factors also show that the assembled forcing vanishes almost everywhere off the support of \rho.

Induction on the order combines the H^2 theorem with the cutoff lemma. The coefficient hypotheses grow with the order, since each differentiation of the equation moves one derivative onto a^{ij}, while the conclusion remains local and free of boundary conditions.

Let m\geq0, let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open, and suppose u\in H^1(\Omega) is a weak solution of

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j u)=f.

Assume the coefficient matrix has globally Lipschitz representatives for the H^2 base step. More precisely, the theorem takes a coefficient field with entries in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n), requires its almost-everywhere ellipticity hypothesis on all of \mathbb R^n, and requires its restriction to \Omega to agree with one coherent W^{m+1,\infty}(\Omega) bundle. If f\in W^{m,2}(\Omega), then every compact K\subset\Omega has an open neighborhood V with K\subset V\subset\Omega on which u has a W^{m+2,2}(V) representative. No trace or boundary condition is imposed on u.

    Finite-order interior regularity for a general weak divergence-form solution.

    The coefficient matrix is represented globally by Lipschitz functions for the H² base case and by one coherent W^{m+1,∞}(Omega) bundle for the higher-order bootstrap. The forcing is represented by one W^{m,2}(Omega) bundle.

Proof for Theorem 5.181
uses 0

The case m=0 is the compact-set H^2 theorem. For the successor step, first apply the induction hypothesis on an intermediate neighborhood of K, then restrict the weak equation and all Sobolev coefficient and forcing data to that neighborhood. A cutoff equal to one near K localizes the equation, with commutator forcing at the required Sobolev order. Apply the preceding-order regularity theorem to each differentiated localized field, then assemble those first derivatives to gain one order for the localized solution. Restricting once more to the cutoff-one region removes the cutoff and yields the claimed W^{m+3,2} representative of the original solution.

The global theory takes a different route. Rather than shrinking to compact subsets, it localizes with the finite partition of unity of an atlas, and the interior piece is proved with a difference-quotient theorem whose coefficients live on all of \mathbb R^n. The PDE only provides coefficients on \Omega, so an extension lemma preserving Lipschitz bounds and ellipticity is needed first.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded with the operational C^1 extension atlas. If the entries of a are globally C^1 and

\xi^\mathsf{T}a(x)\xi\geq\alpha|\xi|^2 \qquad (x\in\Omega,\ \alpha>0),

then there exist one globally defined extension, entrywise Lipschitz constants, and compatible L^\infty(\mathbb R^n) coefficient classes. The pointwise field agrees with a on \Omega, each entry is globally Lipschitz, the L^\infty classes represent those entries almost everywhere, and the resulting matrix is uniformly elliptic with constant \alpha/2.

    A C¹ coefficient field which is uniformly elliptic on a bounded domain admits a globally Lipschitz, globally bounded, uniformly elliptic extension which agrees with it on the domain.

    The extension is uniformly elliptic with constant alpha / 2. It turns coefficient assumptions on the domain into the whole-space coefficients used by the difference-quotient proof.

Proof for Theorem 5.182
uses 0

Continuity extends the ellipticity lower bound from \Omega to its closure and preserves half of it on an open neighborhood. A smooth cutoff equal to one on the compact closure glues a there to the scalar matrix (\alpha/2)I outside that neighborhood. Entrywise compact support of the deviation from (\alpha/2)I gives global Lipschitz bounds and bounded L^\infty representatives, while convexity of the quadratic-form lower bound preserves ellipticity through the transition region.

With the extension in hand, the interior cutoff of the atlas localizes the weak solution away from the boundary. The resulting statement is a zero-trace specialization of the compact-set theorem, phrased so that it can be summed with the boundary pieces.

Proof for Theorem 5.183
uses 0

A compactly supported cutoff localizes the weak equation away from the boundary. Difference quotients give a uniform weighted L^2 estimate for the first derivatives, weak compactness produces the second weak derivatives, and the coordinate derivatives are assembled into the localized H^2 field.

Near the boundary a different mechanism is required, because difference quotients in the normal direction leave the domain. The C^2 charts flatten each boundary patch to the half-space. Write the transformed equation as -\partial_i(\widetilde a^{ij}\partial_jv)=\widetilde f, absorbing the chart Jacobian into the coefficients and load. Tangential difference quotients control every second derivative with at least one tangential index. To see how the last derivative is recovered, expand the equation and isolate the normal direction, indexed here by n:

\widetilde a^{nn}\partial_{nn}v =-\widetilde f -\sum_{(i,j)\ne(n,n)}\widetilde a^{ij}\partial_{ij}v -\sum_{i,j}(\partial_i\widetilde a^{ij})\partial_jv.

Every term on the right is already controlled in L^2. Transformed ellipticity gives \widetilde a^{nn}\ge\widetilde\alpha>0, so division recovers \partial_{nn}v in L^2. For a weak solution the expansion is justified through the normal flux, without assuming the missing derivative exists. The formula explains both the ellipticity hypothesis and the coefficient derivatives needed by the boundary theorem.

    Local boundary regularity in physical coordinates, our counterpart of (71) in step 10 of Evans's proof of §6.3.2, Theorem 4.

    For a bounded domain equipped with C2BoundaryAtlas, uniformly elliptic principal coefficients admitting global C¹ representatives, and an L² forcing term, every boundary partition piece of a weak Dirichlet solution belongs to H²(Ω). The flattened equation, geometric ellipticity constants, odd reflection, and chart pullback are all discharged internally.

Proof for Theorem 5.184
uses 0

Flatten the boundary chart, transport the weak equation and ellipticity, estimate tangential difference quotients, recover the normal derivative from the normal flux, oddly reflect the zero-trace field, pull it back through the C^2 chart, and restrict it to the physical domain.

The interior piece and the finitely many boundary pieces together account for the whole solution, since the atlas cutoffs sum to one on \Omega. Their sum is the global H^2 representative of the principal problem.

    Principal-part case of the qualitative H² regularity of Evans's §6.3.2, Theorem 4.

    On a bounded domain equipped with C2BoundaryAtlas, an H¹₀ weak solution of a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation with principal coefficients admitting global C¹ representatives and with L² forcing has an H²(Ω) representative. Boundary.HasContDiffGraphBoundary.exists_c2BoundaryAtlas constructs this operational atlas from a C² graph boundary.

    This declaration treats b = 0 and c = 0. The full lower-order theorem, including L∞ first- and zeroth-order coefficients, is exists_global_h2_of_weak_shifted_full_divergence_solution.

Proof for Theorem 5.185
uses 0

Construct the interior piece and every boundary-chart piece, then assemble their finite partition of unity in H^2. Equality of each Sobolev base coordinate with its localized weak solution makes the assembled base coordinate equal to the original H^1_0 function almost everywhere.

Lower-order terms and the Gårding shift do not change the argument at this level. Because the solution already lies in H^1_0(\Omega) and the coefficients b^i, c are essentially bounded, the terms b^iD_iu, cu, and \lambda u can be absorbed into an L^2 forcing, reducing the shifted full-operator problem to the principal case.

    The qualitative part of Evans's §6.3.2, Theorem 4, for the full shifted divergence-form operator.

    On a domain equipped with the operational C2BoundaryAtlas, a homogeneous Dirichlet weak solution of

    -∂ᵢ(aᵢⱼ ∂ⱼu) + bᵢ ∂ᵢu + c u + λu = f

    has an H²(Ω) representative when the principal coefficients are W^{1,∞} with global ambient C¹ representatives, the lower-order coefficients are L∞, and f ∈ L²(Ω). The lower-order terms are absorbed into the L² effective forcing using the given H¹₀ solution.

    Setting λ = 0 gives the full operator of Evans's Theorem 4. Boundary.HasContDiffGraphBoundary.exists_c2BoundaryAtlas derives the operational atlas from a C² graph boundary.

Proof for Theorem 5.186
uses 1

Move b\cdot Du, cu, and \lambda u to the right. Since the supplied weak solution lies in H^1_0 and the coefficients are essentially bounded, the effective forcing remains in L^2. Apply principal-part global H^2 regularity to that equation.

5.6.1.3. Higher Orders🔗

Higher regularity differentiates the localized equation and repeatedly uses the derivatives obtained at the preceding step. The global H^2 theorem is the base case. At each higher order we must control both the differentiated forcing and the terms created by differentiating the coefficients. The arbitrary-order theorems record that induction, for the principal operator and for the full operator; their k=1 and k=2 specializations give the traditional H^3 and H^4 statements.

For m\ge1, suppose u\in H^{m+1} is already known, f\in H^m, and a^{ij}\in W^{m+1,\infty}. Differentiating once in coordinate k gives

-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_j(\partial_k u)) =\partial_k f+\sum_{i,j}\partial_i((\partial_k a^{ij})\partial_j u).

The right side belongs to H^{m-1} by the Sobolev product rules. Applying the preceding-order regularity theorem to this equation gives \partial_k u\in H^{m+1}; assembling the first derivatives yields u\in H^{m+2}. Interior cutoffs supply the zero-trace conditions needed for this argument. At a physical boundary, only tangential differentiation preserves zero trace, so normal-flux recovery and pure-normal assembly are separate parts of the induction (Evans, 2010, Theorem 5, pp. 340–343).

    The qualitative part of Evans's §6.3.2, Theorem 5, for the principal operator.

    On a bounded domain equipped with C2BoundaryAtlas and boundary charts of the indicated orders, forcing in W^{k,2} and principal coefficients in W^{k+1,∞} with global C^{k+1} representatives promote an H¹₀ weak solution to W^{k+2,2}. Boundary.HasContDiffGraphBoundary.exists_higherOrderBoundaryAtlas constructs such an atlas from a C^{k+2} graph boundary.

Proof for Theorem 5.187
uses 0

Strong induction begins with global H^2. At a successor order, the previous representative supplies the lower regularity needed to differentiate the localized equation. Interior differentiated equations and flattened boundary equations produce the next localized Sobolev pieces; tangential derivatives, normal-flux recovery, coefficient reciprocals, and pure-normal assembly recover all derivative directions. A finite partition of unity closes the global step.

    The qualitative part of Evans's §6.3.2, Theorem 5, for the full shifted divergence-form operator.

    On a domain with the operational boundary atlas and chart regularity of the indicated orders, forcing in W^{k,2}, principal coefficients in W^{k+1,infinity}, and lower-order coefficients in W^{k,infinity} promote every homogeneous-Dirichlet weak solution from H¹₀ to W^{k+2,2}. No regularity above H¹₀ is assumed for the weak solution.

Proof for Theorem 5.188
uses 0

Use strong induction on k. The base case is full-operator global H^2 regularity. At a successor order, the induction hypothesis supplies the preceding Sobolev representative. The higher-order multiplier estimates then put b\cdot Du, cu, and \lambda u in the required Sobolev space, so the effective forcing belongs to W^{k,2}. Apply the arbitrary-order principal theorem to the rewritten divergence equation.

5.6.1.4. From Sobolev Regularity to Classical Smoothness🔗

The arbitrary-order bootstrap produces an H^{m+2}(\Omega) representative for every finite m. These representatives are initially defined only up to null sets and may depend on m, so this family alone is not yet one classical function. The supercritical Sobolev–Morrey theory resolves that coherence problem both in the interior and on the domain closure.

In every positive dimension, the operational Sobolev theory raises W^{m+n+1,2}(\Omega) to W^{m+1,2n}(\Omega). When n=1, this is simply a restriction from W^{m+2,2} to W^{m+1,2}. In higher dimensions, the first-order extension and Sobolev iteration raise the integrability exponent to 2n. Since 2n>n, the Morrey representatives are continuous, and their compatible weak derivatives are ordinary Fréchet derivatives on the open set. Near a boundary point, an operational chart flattens the closure to a closed half-space. Mathlib's derivative-extension theorem on a convex half-ball then identifies the same continuous derivative field as the derivative within \overline\Omega.

The all-order principal data fix one pointwise coefficient matrix and one pointwise forcing function. Every forward and inverse boundary chart is smooth; the coefficient matrix has a globally smooth representative; for each k, a W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega) coefficient bundle represents that same matrix; and a W^{k,2}(\Omega) forcing bundle represents that same forcing.     Every finite Sobolev order has a classical representative on the closure of an operational smooth domain.

    The proof first raises the exponent to the supercritical value 2n, then applies completed-space Morrey reconstruction. No order-k extension operator or boundary-reconstruction hypothesis is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 5.190
uses 0

For n=1, restrict the derivative order once. For n\geq2, lower the exponent to one, perform n-1 subcritical steps to reach exponent n, and apply the critical embedding with finite target exponent 2n. Since 2n>n, higher-order Morrey embedding supplies continuous representatives for the weak derivatives. The closure weak-to-classical theorem reconstructs their Fréchet derivatives within \overline\Omega.

Applied to the all-orders elliptic bootstrap, the embedding yields a C^m representative for every m. Since all these representatives agree almost everywhere with the same u and are continuous, they coincide on \Omega, which produces one smooth function.

Proof for Theorem 5.191
uses 0

The all-order elliptic bootstrap supplies a representative in every finite Sobolev order. For requested classical order m, Sobolev iteration gives a W^{m+1,2n} representative. Higher-order Morrey embedding produces continuous representatives for the weak derivatives, and the weak-to-classical reconstruction theorem identifies adjacent representatives as Fréchet derivatives on \Omega. Almost-everywhere agreement and continuity identify the representatives pointwise, so one function belongs to C^m(\Omega) for every finite m.

The same coincidence argument extends to the closure. The closure-level embedding provides representatives in C^m(\overline\Omega), and pointwise agreement on \Omega between functions continuous on \overline\Omega persists on \overline\Omega.

    Under smooth compatible charts and coefficients, all-order compatible forcing, and uniform ellipticity, the weak solution has one representative that is infinitely differentiable on the closure and agrees almost everywhere with the original H¹₀ solution. Proof for Theorem 5.192
uses 0

Apply arbitrary-order elliptic regularity at every finite order. The completed-space embedding theorem gives a C^m(\overline\Omega) representative for each m. Any two representatives agree almost everywhere with the same solution; continuity first upgrades this to pointwise equality on \Omega and then on its closure. One representative therefore has every finite derivative order on \overline\Omega.

5.6.2. Bounded Solution Operators🔗

5.6.2.1. Regularity as a bounded operator🔗

An existence theorem may say that every forcing f has a solution with two additional weak derivatives. For linear PDE, one wants more: the chosen solution should depend linearly and continuously on f. Uniqueness of the underlying weak Dirichlet problem makes the choice canonical, and the closed graph theorem supplies continuity once qualitative regularity has been established.

The resulting operators S_2:L^2(\Omega)\to H^2(\Omega) and S_{m+2}:H^m(\Omega)\to H^{m+2}(\Omega) solve the principal divergence-form Dirichlet problem, under the boundary-chart, coefficient, and ellipticity hypotheses of the corresponding global regularity theorems.

    Qualitative elliptic regularity for the weak solution operator at forcing order m.

    This is the hypothesis of the closed-graph construction higherSolutionOperator: every H^m forcing has an H^{m+2} representative of its weak solution.

The predicate is purely qualitative: it asserts the existence of an H^{m+2} representative for each datum and says nothing about how that representative depends on the datum. Linearity and continuity are consequences, the former because a Sobolev field on an open set is determined by its base coordinate, the latter by the closed graph theorem.

✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega be open, let S:L^2(\Omega)\to H^1_0(\Omega) be a bounded linear weak solver, and suppose every H^m datum has an H^{m+2} representative whose base coordinate is the weak solution Sf. Uniqueness of Sobolev fields from their base coordinate makes this qualitative lift linear. Its graph is closed because both the Sobolev base-coordinate map and the weak solver are continuous. The closed graph theorem therefore gives a canonical bounded linear map

S_{m+2}:H^m(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^{m+2}(\Omega),

whose base coordinate is exactly the original weak solution and whose norm obeys the usual operator-norm estimate. The construction uses nothing about the coefficients, which enter only through the lift hypothesis.

    The higher-order solution operator represents the original weak solution.

The first concrete instance takes m=0. The global H^2 theorem supplies the qualitative lift for the principal divergence-form weak solver, and the generic construction turns it into a bounded operator from L^2(\Omega) to H^2(\Omega).

Under the hypotheses of the global H^2 theorem, the canonical weak Dirichlet solver lifts to a bounded linear map

S_2:L^2(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^2(\Omega).

Its value is the unique H^2 representative of the weak solution.

    The global H² solution operator.

    On a bounded domain equipped with C2BoundaryAtlas, with uniformly elliptic principal coefficients admitting global C¹ representatives, the homogeneous-Dirichlet weak solution depends boundedly and linearly on its L² forcing datum, with values in H²(Ω). The operator norm is a constant for the estimate ‖u‖_{H²(U)} ≤ C ‖f‖_{L²(U)} of Remark (i) after Evans's §6.3.2, Theorem 4, for an operator without lower-order terms.

    Restricting the global H² solution to H¹ gives the canonical weak Dirichlet solution.

Continuity of a linear map between normed spaces is the same as an operator-norm inequality, so the estimate is a restatement of boundedness.

For every f\in L^2(\Omega), the canonical solution satisfies

\lVert S_2f\rVert_{H^2(\Omega)} \le\lVert S_2\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\, \lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}.

The constant is independent of the forcing datum.

Proof for Theorem 5.196
uses 0

The regularity and uniqueness argument has already bundled the solver as a continuous linear map S_2:L^2(\Omega)\to H^2(\Omega). The conclusion is exactly the defining operator-norm inequality \lVert S_2f\rVert\leq\lVert S_2\rVert\lVert f\rVert.

The all-orders theorem supplies the qualitative lift for every m, under the correspondingly stronger chart and coefficient hypotheses.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

For every m\in\mathbb N, the all-orders qualitative theorem and uniqueness of the weak solution produce a bounded linear map

S_{m+2}:H^m(\Omega)\longrightarrow H^{m+2}(\Omega)

under the corresponding chart, coefficient, and ellipticity assumptions. The weak H^1_0 solver uses the canonical order-one restriction of the W^{m+1,\infty} coefficient bundle, while the unreduced bundle supplies the derivatives used by the regularity theorem. The base-coordinate identity characterizes the result without unfolding either restriction or the closed-graph construction.

Proof for Theorem 5.198
uses 0

Qualitative regularity gives a unique higher-order representative for each forcing. Linearity follows from uniqueness of the base weak solution, and a closed-graph argument upgrades the resulting linear map to a continuous linear map. Its standard operator-norm inequality is the asserted estimate.

Evolution problems apply elliptic regularity at each time to a residual that depends on time. Given a Bochner trajectory of weak solutions, the stationary operator can be applied at almost every t, and the questions are measurability of the result and control of its norm.

Let the right-hand side belong to L^2(\mu;H^m)\cap L^\infty(\mu;H^m) and the given weak-solution trajectory belong to L^2(\mu;H^1_0). Assume the generic higher-order solver is available and the weak-solution identity holds almost everywhere. Then there exists a trajectory in L^2(\mu;H^{m+2})\cap L^\infty(\mu;H^{m+2}) whose base coordinate agrees almost everywhere with the original weak solution and which obeys the operator-norm estimate. The L^2 memberships are separate hypotheses because the time measure may be infinite.

    Lift an almost-everywhere family of weak elliptic solutions to one L∞_t H^{m+2}_x trajectory.

    The hypothesis identifies the base coordinate of the given H¹₀(Omega)-valued trajectory with the weak solution selected by S for the right-hand side r(t). The conclusion collects the pointwise regularity theorem into a single Bochner class and retains both the almost-everywhere identification and its uniform norm estimate.

    For the wave equation, the caller takes r = f - u_tt; the weak wave identity proves hweak, and the differentiated induction estimate proves hr.

Proof for Theorem 5.199
uses 0

Apply the stationary higher-order solution operator at almost every time. The weak-solution identity and uniqueness identify its base coordinate with the original trajectory. Measurability of the lifted map and the stationary operator-norm bound give the Bochner representative, its essential-supremum estimate, and the asserted almost-everywhere compatibility.

The trajectory statement is an existence result. Behind it stands an operator: the stationary solution operator lifts to a bounded linear map between Bochner spaces, which is the object that the higher-regularity argument for the wave equation composes with.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

For any measure \mu on time, the generic higher-order solver acts on Bochner trajectories as a bounded linear map

L^2(\mu;H^m(\Omega)) \longrightarrow L^2(\mu;H^{m+2}(\Omega)).

It agrees almost everywhere with pointwise application of the stationary solver, and its Sobolev base coordinate is almost everywhere the corresponding weak solution. If \lVert r(t)\rVert_{H^m}\leq C almost everywhere, then the lifted trajectory belongs to L^\infty(\mu;H^{m+2}) and satisfies

\lVert S_{m+2}r(t)\rVert_{H^{m+2}} \leq \lVert S_{m+2}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\,C

almost everywhere.

Proof for Theorem 5.200
uses 0

Lift the stationary continuous linear map pointwise to Bochner L^2. The standard functorial construction gives boundedness and almost-everywhere agreement with pointwise application. Composing with the base-coordinate map yields the weak solution identity. Finally, the stationary operator-norm bound applied almost everywhere preserves the assumed L^\infty envelope.
